label: E5
title: The cell, membranes, proteins and receptors

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A cell is the smallest unit of a living thing, and cells are the basic building blocks of all organisms.

The nucleus houses the cell’s DNA. Ribosomes build proteins. Mitochondria are responsible for making adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which is the cell’s main energy-carrying molecule.

A phospholipid has a head area that is hydrophilic, meaning water-loving: it mixes with water, and a tail area that is hydrophobic, meaning water-hating: it does not. In water these molecules arrange themselves with their hydrophobic tails facing each other and their hydrophilic heads facing out.

The plasma membrane controls the passage of organic molecules, ions, water and oxygen into and out of the cell. Sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and proteins are among those organic molecules.

A protein’s shape is critical to its function, and many different types of chemical bond maintain that shape. Changes in temperature, acidity or exposure to chemicals may change the shape permanently, which loses the function. Enzymes are proteins that act as catalysts in biochemical reactions.

A ligand is a molecule that binds another specific molecule, in some cases delivering a signal in the process. Receptors are protein molecules in the target cell or on its surface that bind ligand, and a specific ligand typically has a specific receptor that binds only that ligand. The cytoplasm is the cell’s whole region between the plasma membrane and the nucleus. It is mostly water but semi-solid. Internal receptors sit in the cytoplasm and respond to hydrophobic ligand molecules that are able to travel across the plasma membrane. Cell-surface receptors span the plasma membrane and perform signal transduction, by which a signal outside the cell is converted into a signal inside it. Binding changes the shape of the receptor, and the changed shape is what does the work.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Everything alive is made of cells.

A cell is a bag of watery jelly, called the cytoplasm, with a skin round it. The skin has a name: the plasma membrane.

The nucleus is the compartment that holds the cell’s instructions, which are written in its DNA.

The ribosomes are the machines that build proteins.

The mitochondria make a small molecule called adenosine triphosphate, written ATP, which the cell uses to carry energy from one reaction to another.

The membrane is built out of one kind of molecule, and that molecule has two ends that behave differently. One end mixes with water. The other end will not mix with water and mixes with grease instead.

Put a lot of them in water and they sort themselves out. The water-hating ends turn inwards and huddle together, away from the water. The water-loving ends turn outwards, where the water is. What you get is a sheet two molecules thick.

So a membrane is wet on both faces and greasy in the middle.

A molecule that dissolves in grease can slip through the greasy middle on its own. A molecule that dissolves in water cannot, and has to be carried across. The carrying is done by proteins that sit in the membrane and take things through.

A protein is a chain. The links of the chain are called amino acids, and there is a small fixed set of kinds. The chain folds up into a shape, and the shape is decided by the order of the links.

The shape is what the protein does. Not the chain, the shape. Change the shape and you change what it does, and a shape that is pulled apart far enough stops working altogether. Heat does that. So does acid.

An enzyme is a protein that makes one particular reaction go faster. It works because of its shape: the thing it acts on fits into it. Every enzyme speeds its reaction up.

Some proteins are shaped so that one particular molecule fits into them. The molecule that fits is called the ligand. The protein it fits into is called the receptor.

When the ligand sits in the receptor, the receptor changes shape. The new shape does something the old shape could not do.

A water-hating ligand crosses the membrane on its own, so its receptor can sit inside the cell. A water-loving ligand cannot cross, so its receptor sits in the membrane itself, sticking out on both sides. The ligand lands on the outside end and never enters. The inside end changes shape and carries the message in.

blocks.label: Illustration
blocks.html:
Nearly everyone who has met the membrane once remembers the phrase selectively permeable. Go and find it.

Open OpenStax Biology 2e, section 5.1, Components and Structure, at https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/5-1-components-and-structure. Open your browser’s find box. Type the words selectively permeable and press enter.

Nothing. The section that describes the membrane does not use the phrase anywhere.

Now search the same page for the word exclude. One sentence comes up.

Cells exclude some substances, take in others, and excrete still others, all in controlled quantities.

It says the membrane picks.

Take a glass of water. Pour in a spoonful of cooking oil. Stir it hard, then stop and watch. The oil comes back together and sits apart from the water.

Now read the phospholipid paragraph on the page you already have open, with that glass in front of you.

…phospholipids arrange themselves with their hydrophobic tails facing each other and their hydrophilic heads facing out.

Draw the result on paper. Two rows of molecules. Tails pointing at each other in the middle, heads facing out on both sides.

Open section 9.1, Signaling Molecules and Cellular Receptors, at https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/9-1-signaling-molecules-and-cellular-receptors. Search inside it for the word hydrophobic.

…respond to hydrophobic ligand molecules that are able to travel across the plasma membrane.

Water-hating molecules travel across the membrane.

A signal arriving at a cell is a molecule. The word for it is the ligand, which means the thing that binds. The protein it binds to is the receptor.

Take any claim that a substance acts on the body and ask three questions in order. What is the molecule? What does it bind? What changes when it binds?

The third question is the one that does the work. A claim that cannot answer it has described something that was present, not something that acted.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The glass of oil and water gets you the greasy middle and nothing else. A membrane is not a puddle.

Water-hating in, water-loving out is a rule with real exceptions, and the book says so itself. The membrane controls the passage of water too, and water is the most water-loving thing there is. Take the rule as telling you what usually crosses unaided, not as a law about every molecule.

The key-in-a-lock picture for a ligand and a receptor breaks in two places. A lock does not change shape when the key turns, and a receptor does, and that change is the entire point. And one key can open more than one kind of lock here: the same signal can reach several kinds of cell.

Binding and acting are not the same event. Something can sit in a receptor and do nothing, and something can sit in it and stop the usual ligand getting in.

This whole section is about what can happen and never about how much. Any question that has a number in its answer is outside it.

points.html: A substance being present in a tissue is not the same as it acting there. So ask which cells carry the receptor before you accept any claim about where a medicine works.
Ask three questions of every mechanism claim, in this order. What is the molecule, what does it bind, and what changes when it binds.
Binding and acting are two claims, not one. A molecule can sit in a receptor and do nothing, or sit in it and keep the usual ligand out.
A protein’s shape is what it does, so anything that changes the shape changes the job. So before you accept that a protein can be given by mouth, ask what the stomach does to it.
Refuse any claim that a mechanism settles whether an effect is big enough to matter. A mechanism tells you what can happen and never how much.
When a product claims to work at the cellular level, ask what it binds and what changes when it does. The phrase names no molecule and no receptor, so it commits to nothing.

Teach the two receptor places before you teach a single drug. A water-hating signal crosses the membrane and meets its receptor inside; everything else is handled by a receptor built through the wall.
An enzyme makes one reaction go faster, and its shape is the reason. Ask which enzyme, and ask how the rate was measured.

blocks.prompt:
Without looking back, write down what happens from the moment a signal molecule reaches a cell to the moment something changes inside it. Do it twice: once for a water-hating signal and once for a water-loving one.

Then say, in one sentence, why the two go different ways.
blocks.answer:
The water-hating signal first. It dissolves in grease, so it crosses the middle of the membrane on its own. Inside the cell it meets its receptor, which is waiting in the jelly. It fits into it. The receptor changes shape. The new shape does a job the old shape could not.

Now the water-loving signal. It cannot cross the greasy middle, so it never enters. Its receptor is built right through the membrane, with one end outside and one end inside. The signal lands on the outside end and stays there. The receptor changes shape. The inside end, now a different shape, starts something happening inside the cell.

Why the two go different ways. The middle of the membrane is greasy. So what dissolves in grease goes through, and what dissolves in water does not.

One thing to check in your own answer. Did you write the shape change in both versions? That is the event. A version that stops at “it binds” has left out the part that does the work.

blocks.prompt:
A company sheet for a herbal capsule says this.

The active molecule has been shown to bind the same receptor as the prescription medicine. It therefore has the same action, without the side effects.

Say what is wrong, and say what you would ask for. The capsule and the sheet are made up for this exercise.
blocks.answer:
Take the two sentences separately, because the first one may well be true and the second does not follow from it.

The first sentence is a binding claim. It says the molecule fits into that receptor. On its own that is checkable and it may be right.

The second sentence is an action claim, and it is a different claim. A ligand binds a receptor, and in some cases delivers a signal in the process. In some cases. Three things can happen when a molecule sits in a receptor. It can change the shape the way the usual ligand does, and the usual thing happens. It can change it some other way. Or it can sit there, change nothing, and keep the usual ligand out, so less happens than before.

The sheet has picked the first of those three and reported it as though binding settled it. Nothing in a binding result chooses between them.

The last clause is a third claim again. Side effects come from everywhere else the molecule goes and everything else it binds. A sheet that has measured one receptor has measured nothing about the rest. “No side effects” from that evidence is a claim about what nobody looked for.

What to ask for. First, what happened downstream in a cell that carries the receptor, not just whether binding occurred. Second, what else the molecule binds. Third, at what amount the binding was seen, and whether a person taking the capsule reaches it.

And say the size point out loud, because it is the one that gets waved through. Binding at some concentration in a dish tells you the shapes fit. It does not tell you the effect is big enough to matter in a person.

blocks.prompt:
A first-year resident has ten minutes and a whiteboard. They can recite that insulin acts on cells, and they cannot say what “acts on” means.

Teach them the membrane and the receptor so that they leave able to place a drug they have never met.
blocks.answer:
Ten minutes, a whiteboard, and somebody who wants a mechanism rather than a rule.

Draw the membrane first, and draw it as two rows of lollipops with the sticks pointing at each other. Heads out on both sides, sticks meeting in the middle. Then write two words on the board: wet outside, greasy inside. Do not say anything about drugs yet.

Ask them which of two molecules gets through on its own: one that dissolves in water, or one that dissolves in oil. They will get it right, because you have drawn the answer. That is the moment to stop and let them see they have just derived something rather than been told it.

Now put a receptor on the board. Draw a shape with a notch in it and a small molecule that fits the notch. Say the two names once: the small molecule is the ligand, the notched protein is the receptor.

Then draw the same protein again with the ligand sitting in the notch, and draw it a different shape. That second drawing is the whole lesson. The event is not the arrival. The event is the shape change.

Now put the two ideas together and let them do it. Ask where the receptor has to be for an oil-loving signal, and where it has to be for a water-loving one. They will place the first inside the cell and the second through the wall. They have now built the general rule themselves.

Place the one they came in with. Insulin’s receptors sit on the cell membrane, so insulin is a signal of the second kind: it lands outside and never needs to enter.

Close with the thing you want them using on Monday. When they meet a new drug, three questions, in order. What is the molecule. What does it bind. What changes when it binds. Tell them the third question is the one that is usually missing. A drug they cannot answer it for is a drug they do not yet understand.
